info.name: 20 · Response-level notes
info.description:
**Response-level notes** (surfaced in the review view): free-text notes an annotator attaches to a selection of one conversation's messages, so a reviewer's reasoning lives next to the transcript it is about.

**The asymmetry this collection is built around.** Notes are deliberately **not** scoped the same way on the two sides:

| | rule |
|---|---|
| **create** | group **visibility** only — there is *no* `Conversation.user_id == caller` predicate, so an annotator can leave a note on a red-teamer's transcript. That is the entire point of the feature. |
| **read / update / delete** | **owner-scoped** — a caller sees only what *they* authored. The conversation's own owner does **not** see an annotator's notes. |
| **break-glass** | `evaluation_groups:manage` (admin) lifts the read scope, but **not** the create path — a manager who cannot see the group cannot author in it either. |

Contrast the sibling: `MessageFlag` keeps the ownership predicate on create (a flag is attributed to its author, so a manager must not stamp one in someone else's name — see `06`).

**Flow.** A) a red teamer holds a conversation with a message worth noting; B) the **annotator** notes it, then reads/updates/lists its own work; C) the **owner-scoped read** — the conversation owner sees nothing, the admin sees everything; D) `notes:*` gating — the `owner` role holds none of it; E) delete, including the cross-author 404.

**Permissions.** `notes:read|create|update|delete` are held by **admin, red_teamer and annotator** — notably **not** by `owner`, which is why folder D's 403 is a role check and not a scope check.

**Contract notes.**
- `message_ids` must all be live messages of the given `conversation_id`; the ancestry (`evaluation_id`, `evaluation_group_id`) is **denormalised onto the row at create** under the caller's visibility, so it cannot drift afterwards.
- Only `text` is editable. To change the selection, create another note.
- Another author's note reads as **404**, never 403 — no existence leak.

**Auth model.** Per-request across four identities. Self-contained; tears down everything but the evaluation group (no DELETE route).

**Prereq.** `make seedlocal`.

**Verified green** — 69/69 assertions, 47 requests, 0 failures, against a live stack whose database has revision `4fd9bfdbdc1f` applied (the annotation→note rename, plus the scenario a conversation now requires). This is also the only end-to-end proof that the renamed **routes and permissions** work against a live stack; the migration's own data rewrites are covered separately, in both directions, by `tests/core/annotations/test_rename_annotations_to_notes.py`.

request.description: Builds the engagement and later demonstrates the `evaluation_groups:manage` break-glass on reads.
Owns the conversation that gets noted — and, in folder C, fails to see the annotator's note on it.
The author of the note. Holds `notes:*` but owns no conversation here.
Holds no `notes:*` at all — folder D's 403.

item.name: 5 · Capture the admin and annotator user ids

exec: pm.test('all three identities resolved', () => { pm.expect(adm).to.be.an('object'); pm.expect(ann).to.be.an('object'); pm.expect(rt).to.be.an('object'); });

request.description: `users:read` (admin). Folders A and B make claims about **who owns what** — that the conversation belongs to the red teamer and the note to the annotator. Without these ids those claims could only be asserted as "is a string", which is true of any author, so the assertions would pass even if the attribution were wrong.
No credential needed — the user turn persists regardless, and that is what gets noted.

**`public` matters.** Create checks *visibility*, so the annotator must be able to see the group without being a member — a public group is the simplest way to arrange that. In an `invitation_only` group the annotator would need an in-group role first.
Evaluations cannot be created under a `pending_approval` group.
The conversation's parent. An note denormalises this id at create time, so folder B asserts it comes back on the row.
Body is `{model_id}`; the response's `id` **is** the assignment id. The assign path re-checks the group's allowed-model subset, so a model outside it would be a 400 here.
Every conversation (group) targets exactly one scenario — the create posts to `/scenarios/{scenario_id}/...` — so the evaluation needs one before folder A starts a conversation.

exec: pm.test('owned by the red teamer, not the admin who built the evaluation', () => { pm.expect(pm.response.json().user_id).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('an_rt_user_id')); pm.expect(pm.response.json().user_id).to.not.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('an_admin_user_id')); });

request.description: A red teamer can start a conversation in any group it can **see** — no membership needed for a `public` group. This conversation is the one the annotator will leave a note on without owning.

exec: pm.test('the stream carried at least one event', () => pm.expect(pm.response.text()).to.include('event:'));

request.description: ⚠ SSE. `client_message_id` must be a UUID (a non-UUID is a 422). With no model credential the assistant turn finalizes to `error`, but the **user** message is `complete` — and a complete message is note-able, which is all this collection needs.

item.name: 3 · Find the message to leave a note on

exec: pm.test('the user turn persisted as complete', () => pm.expect(user.status).to.eql('complete'));

request.description: History is ordered oldest-first across turns. The user message id becomes the note's `message_ids` selection.

item.name: B · The annotator notes someone else's transcript

exec: pm.test('ancestry is denormalised onto the row', () => { pm.expect(b.evaluation_id).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('an_eval_id')); pm.expect(b.evaluation_group_id).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('an_group_id')); });

pm.test('attributed to the annotator, not the conversation owner', () => { pm.expect(b.created_by_id).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('an_annotator_user_id')); pm.expect(b.created_by_id).to.not.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('an_rt_user_id')); });

request.description: **The core of the feature.** The caller does not own this conversation and is not a member of the group — visibility alone is enough. `evaluation_id` / `evaluation_group_id` are resolved once here, under the caller's visibility, so later reads need only the note's own columns and the ancestry cannot drift.
Trivially allowed — the author is inside its own read scope.

exec: pm.test('text updated', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().text).to.eql('Refusal is correct, but it names an internal policy id.'));

request.description: Only `text` is editable — the message selection is immutable, so re-scoping a note means writing a new one.

**FE note:** this is the call the review view makes to render notes beside a transcript. Filters: `conversation_id`, `evaluation_id`, `evaluation_group_id`, `message_id`, `created_by_id`, `created_from`/`created_to`, `search`.

exec: pm.test('the message_id filter finds notes whose selection includes it', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().items.map(i => i.id)).to.include(pm.collectionVariables.get('an_note_id')));

request.description: `message_id` matches notes whose *selection contains* that message — the per-message lookup the transcript uses to place a note against the right bubble.

item.name: 1 · The conversation owner lists — and sees nothing

exec: pm.test('reads are owner-scoped, so the note is invisible to the transcript owner', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().total).to.eql(0));

request.description:
The red teamer **owns the conversation** and holds `notes:read`, and still sees nothing — reads return only what the caller *authored*. Not a bug: a reviewer's private reasoning is not addressed to the person being reviewed.

Worth knowing when reading the FE: a red teamer's note panel shows only their own notes, so "my note vanished" reports are usually a different author, not a lost row.

item.name: 2 · And cannot fetch it by id → 404

request.description: Out-of-scope rows read as *missing*, so addressing one cannot confirm it exists.

item.name: 3 · Admin sees it via the break-glass

exec: pm.test('the manager reads another author\'s note', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().id).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('an_note_id')));

request.description: `evaluation_groups:manage` lifts the **read** scope to every author's work. It does *not* lift the create path — a manager who cannot see the group cannot author an note in it.

item.name: 4 · Admin lists every author's notes on the conversation

exec: pm.test('the break-glass list is not owner-scoped', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().total).to.be.at.least(1));

request.description: The same lift on the list path, so a manager can audit a conversation's whole note history.

item.name: 5 · The transcript owner can still leave a note on it themselves

exec: pm.test('created', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().text).to.eql('My own note on my own transcript.'));

request.description: Owner-scoped reads cut both ways — the red teamer authors its own note and *that* one it can see. A conversation carries many independent notes from many authors.

exec: pm.test('its own note only — the annotator\'s is still hidden', () => { const b = pm.response.json(); pm.expect(b.total).to.eql(1); pm.expect(b.items[0].id).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('an_rt_note_id')); });

request.description: Two notes exist on this conversation (step 5 and folder B); this caller sees one. The pair with folder C step 4 is the whole scoping rule in two requests.

item.name: 1 · The owner role holds no notes:read → 403

exec: pm.test('a permission refusal, not an empty list', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().detail).to.include('notes:read'));

request.description: `notes:*` is held by **admin, red_teamer and annotator** — not `owner`. A **403** rather than an empty page, which is the distinction that matters: the caller is told the capability is missing, not that there is nothing to see.

item.name: 2 · The owner role cannot create either → 403

request.description: The gate is on the route, so it fires before any visibility or ownership logic — and before body validation.

item.name: 3 · The owner role cannot update either → 403

request.description: `notes:update` is a separate member of the split, gated per verb — so it needs its own denial. Note the row *does* exist and the caller could not touch it either way; the 403 proves the refusal is the missing capability, not the owner-scope 404 an eligible role would get.

item.name: 4 · The owner role cannot delete either → 403

request.description: `notes:delete`, likewise. The four members of the split are four independent route gates; a suite that only exercises one of them proves nothing about the other three.
The gate order in full: no credential is a 401 before any permission or scope check runs.
Every `message_ids` entry must be a live message **of that conversation**. A mismatch reads as 404 rather than 422 — the ids are well-formed, they just do not resolve inside the caller's scope.
The annotator holds `notes:delete` but the row is outside its owner-scoped view, so it reads as missing.
Soft delete.
`evaluation_groups:manage` lifts delete as well as read — so a manager can retract a note, though never author one.

exec: pm.test('the conversation has no live notes left', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().total).to.eql(0));

request.description: Checked through the break-glass list, which would still see either row if it had survived.

item.name: F · A soft-deleted parent hides the note
1 · Red teamer starts a second conversation

request.description: A throwaway parent, so the cascade can be exercised without destroying the conversation folders A–E built.
⚠ SSE. Only the persisted **user** turn matters here; the assistant turn errors without a credential.
A live note on a live conversation — the baseline the next step measures against.
Establishes that step 7's 404 is caused by the parent delete and not by the note never having been visible.

item.name: 6 · Naming conv2's message under conv1 → 404 (the foreign case)

exec: pm.test('the message, not the conversation, is what is refused', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().detail.toLowerCase()).to.include('message'));

request.description: The security case `assert_messages_in_conversation` exists for: both ids are **live and real**, they just belong to different conversations. Step D/6 sends a nonexistent id, which the unknown-id branch would refuse anyway — only this one fails if the `Turn.conversation_id` predicate is dropped.

item.name: 7 · Admin deletes the parent conversation group

request.description: Cascade-soft-deletes the group **and** its conversations. Per the service's own docstring no cascade reaches the note row — its disappearance in step 7 comes from the read-side join, not from a write.

item.name: 8 · The note now reads as missing

request.description:
**The regression this folder exists to catch.** No cascade touches the note row itself — the service documents that reads join the **live** ancestor line (conversation → evaluation → group), which is what makes a soft-deleted parent hide it. (The row's own `deleted_at` is not observable through the API, so that half is the code's documented design, not something this request measures; what it measures is the 404.)

A future change that scoped notes by their own `deleted_at` alone would still pass every other assertion in this collection while leaking notes attached to deleted transcripts. This is the repo's recurring soft-delete-cascade bug class, and before this folder existed the suite asserted it nowhere for notes.

item.name: 9 · …and is gone from the list too

exec: pm.test('the list agrees with the detail read', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().total).to.eql(0));

request.description: Both read paths must narrow identically — a list that still returned the row while the detail 404s would be the inconsistency the live-parent join exists to prevent.
Admin can delete the red teamer's conversation group through the `evaluation_groups:manage` break-glass. Cascades to its conversations.
Parent of the conversation group deleted above — children first, then parents.
The evaluation group leaks — no DELETE route; `run_suffix` keeps its title unique.
